content: A stye is an inflamed oil gland located at the edge of the eyelid, where the eyelashes meet the lid. It typically presents as a red, swollen bump resembling a pimple and is tender to the touch. Symptoms of a Stye In addition to the characteristic red, swollen bump, other symptoms may include: A gritty or scratchy sensation, as if a foreign body is present in the eye. Sensitivity to light. Excessive tearing of the eye. Tenderness of the eyelid. Causes of a Stye Styes are caused by bacteria from the skin entering the oil glands in the eyelids, which are responsible for lubricating the tear film. They are similar to acne pimples that occur on other parts of the skin. It is possible to have more than one stye at the same time. Styes usually develop over a few days and may drain and heal on their own. However, a stye can evolve into a chalazion, which occurs when an inflamed oil gland becomes completely blocked. A large chalazion can interfere with vision. Individuals with blepharitis are at a higher risk of developing styes. High-Risk Groups People with blepharitis are more likely to develop styes. Diagnosis A stye can be diagnosed by a doctor through a simple visual examination. Special tests are generally not required. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care You should contact your doctor if: You experience vision problems. The eyelid bump worsens or does not improve within one to two weeks of self-care. The bump becomes very large or painful. You notice a blister on your eyelid. There is crusting or scaling of the eyelids. The entire eyelid or the eye itself becomes red. You are highly sensitive to light or have excessive tearing. A stye recurs shortly after successful treatment of a previous one. The eyelid bump begins to bleed. Treatment Options Styes and chalazions can be treated by applying warm compresses to the affected area for 10 minutes, four times a day. Do not attempt to squeeze a stye or any other eyelid bump. Allow it to drain naturally. Antibiotic creams may be helpful for recurrent or persistent styes. In some cases, large styes may need to be lanced by a healthcare professional to drain the infection. Diseases with Similar Symptoms Other eyelid bumps that may resemble styes include: Xanthelasma: Raised yellow patches on the eyelids, often associated with aging. These are harmless but may occasionally indicate high cholesterol levels. Papillomas: Pink or skin-colored bumps that are benign but may grow slowly, affect vision, or cause cosmetic concerns. They can be surgically removed if necessary. Cysts: Small fluid-filled sacs that can impact vision. Prevention To prevent styes, always wash your hands thoroughly before touching the skin around your eyes. If you are prone to styes, it may help to carefully clean excess oils from the edges of your eyelids. Prognosis Styes often resolve on their own, although they may recur. The prognosis is generally excellent with simple treatment.
